summary: This paper implements and compares three fault-tolerant syndrome extraction strategies for the Steane $[\![7,1,3]\!]$ code: Shor's cat-state method (85–92% preparation success, 96.8% syndrome fidelity), Steane's encoded-ancilla approach (97.8% syndrome fidelity), and a unified CSS scheduler framework. Extensive Qiskit simulations under realistic noise ($p_{\mathrm{phys}}=10^{-3}$) achieve logical error rates as low as $5.1 \times 10^{-5}$ and demonstrate 2.4$\times$ improvement in error suppression compared to standard syndrome extraction.
motivation: Practical quantum error correction hinges on syndrome extraction, but ancilla qubits used for measurement can propagate errors across the system if they fail, destroying the information being protected. This work addresses the fundamental ancilla error propagation problem that threatens the viability of fault-tolerant quantum computing.
method: Three syndrome measurement strategies were implemented in Qiskit with configurable parameters: cat-state ancillas with adjustable verification depth (2–3 parity checks optimal), encoded logical ancillas with adaptive swap policies, and a flexible scheduler enabling hardware-specific mode selection. Benchmarking spans randomized Clifford circuits (depth 2000) and $T$-heavy circuits (82,000 shots) under superconducting noise ($p_{1q}=10^{-3}$, $p_{2q}=10^{-2}$, $p_{\mathrm{meas}}=1.5\%$). Decoding uses majority voting, Viterbi, and Bayesian inference with temporal tracking across distances $d=3$ to $d=13$.
result: Steane encoded-ancilla achieves 97.8% syndrome fidelity with logical error rates of $5.1 \times 10^{-5}$ (20$\times$ suppression) at $p_{\mathrm{phys}}=10^{-3}$; cat-state extraction reaches 96.8% fidelity with 5$\times$ ancilla overhead; threshold analysis reveals exponential error suppression below $p_{\mathrm{phys}} \approx 1\%$, confirming fault-tolerant quantum error correction is viable on current hardware operating $10\times$ below threshold.
